entries.meaning: Rāma said to the sage, ‘Nothing can be hidden from you, Lord. You know why I have come, father, so I did not explain it. Now give me the counsel by which I may slay the enemies of the sages.’ Agastya smiled: ‘Why ask me as though I know anything, Lord? By the power of worshipping you, destroyer of sin, I know only a little of your greatness. Your māyā is a vast cluster-fig tree, its fruits the countless multitudes of universes. Moving and unmoving living creatures dwell within them like insects and know no other reality. Terrible Time devours those fruits, yet even Time forever trembles in fear of you. You are Lord and master of every world, yet ask me as if you were human. I ask this boon, abode of grace: dwell in my heart with Śrī Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, and grant ceaseless devotion, detachment, holy company and unbroken love for your lotus feet. Though your form is infinite, indivisible Brahman, reached in experience and worshipped by saints, I describe and know your form thus and repeatedly delight in the embodied Brahman. You ever give honour to servants; therefore, Rāma, you ask me. There is a supremely lovely and holy place named Pañcavaṭī. Sanctify the Daṇḍaka forest there and release it from the eminent sage's fierce curse. Dwell there, king of Raghu's line, and show compassion to all the sages.’ Receiving permission, Rāma set out and soon neared Pañcavaṭī. He met Jaṭāyu, king of vultures, and deepened their love in many ways. Near the Godāvarī the Lord stayed in a thatched leaf-hut.

From the time Rāma made his dwelling there, the sages became happy and their fear passed away. The beauty of mountains, forests, rivers and lakes spread everywhere, and each day they grew lovelier. Flocks of birds and deer remained joyful, and bees hummed sweetly and gained splendour. Even the serpent king could not describe the forest where Rāma visibly dwelt. Once, as the Lord sat at ease, Lakṣmaṇa spoke without guile: ‘Lord of gods, people, sages and all moving and unmoving life, I ask you as my own master. Explain to me that by which, abandoning everything else, I may serve the dust of your feet. Explain knowledge, detachment and māyā, and the devotion by which you show mercy. Lord, explain fully the distinction between God and the individual soul, so that love for your feet arises and grief, delusion and confusion depart.’

Rāma replied, ‘I shall explain everything briefly; listen, dear brother, fixing intellect, mind and attention upon it. “I and mine, you and yours”—this is māyā, which has subjected multitudes of living beings. Know as māyā everything as far as the senses and their objects and as far as the mind can go. Hear its two divisions: knowledge-māyā and ignorance-māyā. The one is evil, intensely painful, and under its sway the soul has fallen into the well of becoming. The other creates the world and holds the guṇas under its command, but, impelled by the Lord, it has no power of its own. Knowledge is where no pride whatever remains and one sees Brahman equally present in everything. Call one supremely detached who has renounced supernatural attainments and the three guṇas as straw. Call that the individual soul which does not know māyā, God, or its own self. The supreme Lord is the giver of bondage and liberation, transcends all, impels māyā, and is the auspicious boundary of all.’

‘Detachment comes from dharma and knowledge from yoga; the Vedas declare that knowledge gives liberation. But that by which I am quickly moved, brother, is devotion to me, which gives devotees happiness. It is independent and rests on no other support; knowledge and realization depend upon it. Devotion, dear brother, is the incomparable root of happiness, and is found when saints are favourable. I shall describe its disciplines—the easy path by which beings reach me. First comes intense love for the feet of Brahmins, and dedication to one's proper work in the Vedic way. Its fruit is detachment from sense objects; then love for my dharma arises. Firm practice of the nine modes beginning with hearing, deep love in the heart for my divine play, great love for saints' lotus feet, and a firm rule of worship in mind, action and speech follow. One regards teacher, father, mother, kinsman, husband and deity as all present in me and serves firmly. Singing my virtues, one's body thrills, one's voice falters and tears flow from one's eyes. Where desire and its companions, pride and hypocrisy are absent, I, dear brother, dwell continually. Those who selflessly worship me as their refuge in speech, deed and mind—I forever rest within the lotus of their hearts.’

Hearing the yoga of devotion, Lakṣmaṇa felt immense happiness and bowed his head at the Lord's feet. Some days passed in this way as Rāma taught detachment, knowledge, virtue and right conduct. Śūrpaṇakhā, Rāvaṇa's sister, had a cruel, wicked heart like a serpent. One day she came to Pañcavaṭī and, seeing the two princes, became agitated. The verse says that on seeing a handsome man a woman may become agitated and unable to restrain her mind even if he is brother, father or son, just as a sunstone melts on seeing the sun. Assuming an attractive form, she approached the Lord and said with many smiles, ‘There is no man like you and no woman like me; Fate must have thoughtfully created this match. Searching the three worlds, I have seen no man suited to me. Therefore I have remained unmarried until now; seeing you, my mind has somewhat consented.’ Looking toward Sītā, Rāma said his younger brother was unmarried. Knowing her as the enemy's sister, Lakṣmaṇa looked to Rāma and gently replied, ‘Beautiful lady, I am his servant and dependent, so you would have no comfort with me. The Lord is capable, the king of Kosala; whatever he does befits him. A servant who wants comfort, a beggar honour, an addict wealth, an adulterer an auspicious destiny, a greedy person fame, and a proud person the four ends of life are all creatures wishing to milk the sky.’ She returned to Rāma, who again sent her to Lakṣmaṇa. Lakṣmaṇa said, ‘Only he will marry you who breaks with shame as lightly as a straw.’ Enraged, she went back to Rāma and revealed her terrible form. Seeing Sītā afraid, Rāma gave his brother a meaningful signal. With exceptional swiftness Lakṣmaṇa deprived her of nose and ears—like a challenge sent through her hand to Rāvaṇa.

Without nose and ears Śūrpaṇakhā became deformed, like a stream of red ochre pouring from a mountain. Wailing, she went to Khara and Dūṣaṇa and cried, ‘Shame, shame upon your virility and strength, brothers!’ They questioned her; she explained everything, and hearing her the demons assembled an army. Hordes of night-wanderers rushed out like flocks of winged mountains of lampblack, innumerable and terrible, bearing many weapons, riding many vehicles and assuming many forms. They placed Śūrpaṇakhā in front, misshapen and deprived of ears and nose. Countless frightening omens arose, but, all helpless under death, they did not heed them. Roaring, threatening and flying into the sky, the warriors rejoiced greatly at the sight of their army. Some shouted, ‘Capture both brothers alive; after seizing and killing them, carry off the woman.’ Dust filled the vault of heaven. Rāma summoned Lakṣmaṇa and said, ‘Take Jānakī into a mountain cave and remain alert; a terrible army of demons has arrived.’ Hearing the Lord, Lakṣmaṇa departed with Sītā, bow and arrows in hand. Seeing the enemy host advancing, Rāma smiled and strung the formidable Kodaṇḍa bow.
